claims.text: Homogeneous alloy formation in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is controlled by synchronization of precursor reduction kinetics.
Simultaneous reduction of all constituent metal ions causes them to nucleate together.
Joint nucleation produces a compositionally uniform alloy.
Sequential or staggered reduction leads to phase separation and elemental segregation.
Rapid, spatially uniform thermal or chemical activation can synchronize reduction across the metal species.
Synchronized reduction generates uniform nucleation clusters.
Uniform nucleation clusters coalesce into nanoparticles containing a homogeneous distribution of all constituent elements.
Simultaneous reduction minimizes the period during which an individual element can nucleate separately.
Kinetically synchronized nucleation promotes complete atomic-scale mixing and prevents early phase separation.
Kinetically synchronized nucleation encourages formation of a high-entropy alloy with abundant catalytic surface sites.
Relative to staggered reduction, synchronized reduction will produce a more uniform elemental distribution.
Relative to staggered reduction, synchronized reduction will produce smaller, more morphologically controlled nanoparticles.
Relative to staggered reduction, synchronized reduction will enhance catalytic surface area or surface-atom exposure.
A less-controlled, nonsynchronous baseline will undergo sequential nucleation, elemental clustering, phase separation, and irregular morphology.
The proposed mechanism should apply to noble-metal systems whose constituent reduction potentials are not drastically different.
Large differences in precursor reactivity can override the benefits of kinetic synchronization.
Dominant ligand or solvent stabilization effects can make the proposed synchronization mechanism inapplicable.
